messages.text: Hi, I'm starting to read this paper for my project on how non-experts write prompts. Before I get into the findings, could you tell me what the limitations of the study are? I want to know how much I can trust the results, especially the sample size and how the data were analysed.

messages.short_answer: The paper itself names a few limitations: the 10-person sample is skewed toward STEM professionals and graduate students and is not representative, and the sample size was chosen to find easy-to-find usability problems rather than to estimate prevalence. The passages retrieved do not give a detailed account of the data analysis method beyond affinity diagrams and service blueprints, so the analysis side needs more checking.

sections.title: Sample size and who was studied
sections.text: The authors state that ten participants with little to no prompt design experience were recruited, and that the sample size follows prior formative usability work aimed at easy-to-find problems. They also say the pool skews toward STEM professionals and graduate students and is not representative of the population at large.

sections.title: How the data were analysed
sections.text: Two authors compared approaches across participants and categorized struggles using affinity diagrams and a service blueprint. The authors justify these HCI and service-design methods by their focus on discovering opportunities created by a new technology, rather than on a grounded theory approach to established work practices.

sections.title: What this means for your user study
sections.text: A small, non-representative sample with a formative aim means the findings are best read as a rich description of struggles rather than as frequencies or generalizable effects. If your study needs to make claims about non-experts in general, you would likely need a broader and more diverse sample and a stated analysis plan. Consider whether you will also control or document how much help participants receive, since the authors note that advice varied.

sources.text: These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

Systematic testing and robust prompt design—designing prompts that work across many users and many conversations—are by defnition impossible if the user only ever engages in a single conversation, even continuously updated. That said, for some contexts non-robust prompt design can be appropriate: chatbots intended for a single user who is also the designer do not necessarily need to be robust. sources.text: These pages describe a seven-step iterative prompt design workflow used with the BotDesigner tool, in which a user identifies and labels errors in chatbot conversations, debugs them by editing the prompt, and evaluates fixes locally and globally, framed as a regression-test approach that extends prior ad-hoc prompt tools. They then outline a user study with 10 non-expert prompt designers who had little prompt design experience, using think-aloud while improving a baseline chatbot. The study task asked participants to make a cooking chatbot resemble a professional chef from the web series Back to Back Chef, a task chosen over open-ended chatbot creation because pilot users mostly explored capabilities rather than iterating on prompts. The authors note the participant pool is skewed toward STEM professionals and graduate students and is not representative, so they make no claims about general population prevalence. They also note that the sample size follows prior formative usability work aimed at easy-to-find problems.

In this paper, we use chatbots as an example domain to explore the interactions between end user designers and prompt-based systems backed by LLMs (as BotDesigner is). A few additional limitations of our study bear exploration, and point to future studies. First, the reliance on a relatively small pool of likely “early adopters” drawn from academia may skew the observed phenomena towards a specifc set of analogies and preconceived notions around technology and its capabilities. We claim neither that our observations are universal of all end users, nor that they are a complete description of all common misconceptions or behaviors of end-users working with LLM-backed systems. Additionally, the time we gave participants to engage in prompt design was relatively limited, and it is likely that, given enough time and motivation, end users would advance quite quickly in developing better mental models and more efective strategies.

retrieved.text: This excitement around LLMs and prompting is propelling a rapidly growing set of LLM-powered applications [23] and prompt design tools [3, 20, 32]. Yet despite widespread excitement, surprisingly little is known about how non-experts intuitively approach designing prompts with LLM-and-prompt-based tools, and how efective they are in doing so. While prompting LLMs can appear efortless, designing efective prompting strategies requires identifying the contexts in which these LLMs’ errors arise, devising prompting strategies to overcome them, and systematically assessing those strategies’ efectiveness. These tasks fall on so-called “prompt engineers”— the designers, domain experts, and any other end-user or professional attempting to improve an LLM’s output—and are challenging tasks even for LLM experts, as well as topics of ongoing research in Natural Language Processing (NLP) [7, 30, 42]. Prompt design tools to date have focused on supporting professional programmers [45] and NLP practitioners [42], rather than non-AI experts, non-programmers, and other potential end-users of these systems.

Recall that our focus here is understanding end-users in the domain of prompt design; experience in chatbot design was thus not considered grounds for exclusion. Our sample size was chosen in line with prior work around formative testing for usability [19, 43]: our goal is to explore the frst, “easy-to-fnd” problems users encounter when engaged in our task, and our experience with a pilot user suggested that problem discoverability was likely to be high. Our participant pool, skewed towards professionals and graduate students in STEM-related felds, is not representative of the population at large.

Ultimately, our probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming systems and interactive machine learning systems. Expectations stemming from human-to-human instructional experiences, and a tendency to overgeneralize, were barriers to efective prompt design. Why Johnny Can’t Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts J.D. Zamfrescu-Pereira zamf@berkeley.edu UC Berkeley Berkeley, CA, USA Bjoern Hartmann bjoern@eecs.berkeley.edu UC Berkeley Berkeley, CA, USA ABSTRACT Pre-trained large language models (“LLMs”) like GPT-3 can engage in fuent, multi-turn instruction-taking out-of-the-box, making them attractive materials for designing natural language interactions. Using natural language to steer LLM outputs (“prompting”) has emerged as an important design technique potentially accessible to non-AI-experts. Crafting efective prompts can be challenging, however, and prompt-based interactions are brittle. Here, we explore whether non-AI-experts can successfully engage in “end-user prompt engineering” using a design probe—a prototype LLM-based chatbot design tool supporting development and systematic evaluation of prompting strategies. Ultimately, our probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming systems and interactive machine learning systems.

The Playground interface includes over 50 example prompts and enables anyone to experiment with diferent prompts for accomplishing various tasks. Though useful, Playground lacks any support for systematic evaluation of prompts. Propelled by the potential of non-expert prompt design, a rapidly growing set of end-user-facing LLM-based applications is emerging from HCI research, many with features that support prompt engineering. Such applications span across LLM-enhanced story writing and programming [23, 38, 45, 48]. NLP researchers have also started creating tools to enable anyone to contribute prompts to help train LLMs [3, 15]. Interestingly, these tools ofer little to no support for non-experts in generating or evaluating prompts, often assuming that looking at individual input-output pairs in isolation is sufcient. One telling example is AI Chains [49], a tool for exploring human-LLM collaborative writing interactions. AI Chains allows designers to construct a chain of LLMs where the output of one LLM becomes the input for the next, and to test the resulting interactions themselves.

Using this tool as a design probe, we observed how 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience executed a chatbot design task using BotDesigner, to explore a few diferent pieces of this larger question. Our fndings suggest that, while end-users can explore prompt designs opportunistically, they struggle to make robust, systematic progress. Their struggles echo many well-known struggles observed in end-user programming systems (EUPS) and non-expect users of interactive machine learning (iML) systems. Additional barriers to efective prompt design stem from limited conceptions of LLMs’ prompt understanding and execution abilities and their understandable inclinations to design prompts that resemble human-to-human instructions. We discuss these observations’ implications for designing efective end-user-facing LLM-based design tools, implications for education that improves LLM-andprompt literacy among programmers and the general public, and opportunities for further research. This paper makes three contributions.

In this paper, we use chatbots as an example domain to explore the interactions between end user designers and prompt-based systems backed by LLMs (as BotDesigner is). A few additional limitations of our study bear exploration, and point to future studies. First, the reliance on a relatively small pool of likely “early adopters” drawn from academia may skew the observed phenomena towards a specifc set of analogies and preconceived notions around technology and its capabilities. We claim neither that our observations are universal of all end users, nor that they are a complete description of all common misconceptions or behaviors of end-users working with LLM-backed systems. Additionally, the time we gave participants to engage in prompt design was relatively limited, and it is likely that, given enough time and motivation, end users would advance quite quickly in developing better mental models and more efective strategies.

persona_text:
# Persona: Kenji

**Who.** Kenji is a Japanese PhD student in natural language processing (field A) who wants to move into
human-computer interaction (field B) and run user studies, but knows little HCI methodology. He writes
fluent but imperfect English and occasionally asks for a key term to be explained in Japanese.

**What he wants.** To learn how HCI studies people and to judge which of its methods he could borrow for his
project on how non-experts write prompts for LLM-based tools. Reading goal: *Explore potential use in my
research*.

**How he behaves.**
- Writes in English with small grammar mistakes. Interface language: English.
- Is precise about NLP terms but maps HCI concepts onto NLP ones ("so the participants are like the test
  set?", "is the design probe a kind of baseline model?"). Some of these analogies are wrong.
- Changes focus mid-conversation, e.g. from the findings to how the study was run.
- Asks about the strength of the evidence (number of participants, how the data were coded or analysed).
- Checks the sources often.
- Asks for a critical review of whether a method fits his project; his own verdict sometimes differs from
  PaperLens's suggestion.

**Paper.** Why Johnny Can't Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts.
